chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayyoub, from Muhammad ibn Sowqat, who said:
I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the Words of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: 'So whoever alters it after he has heard it, then the sin is upon those who alter it.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'It was abrogated by the verse that follows it, His Words, the Mighty and Majestic: 'But he who fears from the testator an inclination to a wrong course or an act of disobedience, and makes peace between them, then there is no blame on him.'

He said: 'It means the executor; if he fears injustice from the testator regarding what he bequeathed to him, from that which Allah is not pleased with, being contrary to the right, then there is no blame on him, i.e., upon the executor, to alter it to the right and to that which Allah is pleased with, from the way of goodness.'

key_terms.الْمُوصَى إِلَيْهِ: The executor (person to whom the will is addressed)
key_terms.جَنَفاً: Inclination to a wrong course / injustice
key_terms.نَسَخَتْهَا: Abrogated it (rendered it inapplicable by a later verse)

ai.seo_question: How does the executor correct a will if the testator's bequest is unjust or contrary to God's pleasure?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the general prohibition against altering a will is abrogated by the specific provision allowing correction when injustice or sin is feared, establishing a principle of pragmatic flexibility in estate management. This ruling empowers the executor to modify the bequest to align with divine pleasure, ensuring that the testator's intent does not lead to religious or moral error, a concept deeply rooted in Shia jurisprudence regarding the preservation of justice in legal instruments.
